**Weaver Wind Project Hancock County, Maine**

**Prepared For:** Weaver Wind LLC 129 Middle Street Portland, ME  04101

**Prepared By:** Normandeau Associates, Inc. 8 Fundy Road Falmouth, ME  04105

## **List of Tables**

**Page**

**APPENDICES APPENDIX A:** Curtailment Plan

## **1.0 Project Overview**

Weaver Wind LLC (Applicant), a wholly owned subsidiary of First Wind Energy LLC, proposes to construct the Weaver Wind Project (project), a 23-turbine utility scale wind energy facility in Hancock County, Maine.  The project will be constructed on ridges and hills south of Route 9, including Hardwood Hill, Birch Hill, Een Ridge, Little Bull Hill, and other unnamed hills nearby.  The Weaver Wind Project is designed to accommodate two different turbine models:

- Vestas V117-3.3; 116.5 meter hub height and a maximum height of 574 feet; or

- Vestas V126-3.3; 117 meter hub height and a maximum height of 591 feet.

In addition to turbines, project features will include: upgrades to existing roads and construction of new roads ; up to five permanent and up to eight temporary meteorological (met) towers; above and below ground 34.5 kilovolt (kV) electrical collector lines among the turbines (the majority of which will be buried alongside project roads).  The turbines will have an installed capacity of 75.9 megawatts (MW) of electricity.

## **2.0 Post-Construction Avian and Bat Fatality Monitoring Protocol**

Post-construction monitoring will be conducted during the first two years of operation of the Weaver Wind Project to assess wildlife impacts resulting from the project.  The methods detailed within this work plan are based on standard postconstruction monitoring techniques used (and results obtained) at existing wind projects in the State and the region over the past seven years.  This includes available work plans developed in consultation with Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (MDIFW) for the following operational wind facilities: Stetson I, Stetson II, Rollins, Record Hill, and Bull Hill.  Post-construction monitoring efforts assume that the 23 turbines associated with the Weaver Wind Project will be curtailed as described below.

## **2.1 Curtailment**

Research at operating wind facilities indicates that curtailment of wind turbines has the potential to reduce bat mortality.  Curtailment consists of altering (delaying) the operation of a wind turbine so that it begins spinning to generate energy at a wind

speed greater than its normal “cut-in” wind speed.   For example, the turbine blades will begin spinning and the generator will begin producing electricity once wind speeds reach 5.0 meters per second (m/s) rather than the typical 3.0 or 3.5 m/s.  The documented reduction in bat fatality rates at these cut-in speeds reflects data that indicate that activity (foraging, migrating, swarming, etc.) decreases significantly as wind speed increases beyond the 3 to 5 m/s range.

The Applicant proposes to curtail operation of the Weaver Wind Project to reduce potential bat fatalities.  Turbines will operate only at cut-in wind speeds exceeding 5.0 m/s each night (from sunset to sunrise) during the period of July 1 through September 30, which is the demonstrated peak period of bat fatalities at projects in Maine and throughout the Northeast (Appendix A).

The curtailment plan for the project is based the most current available data from post-construction fatality monitoring and curtailment assessment studies in Maine and across North America.  The curtailment plan proposed for the project differs from the recommendations in the _Maine Turbine Curtailment Requirements to Decrease Bat Mortality Policy_ (MDIFW, January 2014).  The proposed deviations from the MDIFW guidelines are based on the following: (1) the curtailment parameters recommended by MDIFW exceed the parameters that have been determined to reliably reduce bat fatalities in several studies; and (2) the curtailment guidelines from MDIFW would result in an unnecessary cost to the project and loss of renewable energy generation without providing demonstrated reduction in bat fatalities.  Further details regarding the propose curtailment plan and associated justification are provided in Appendix A of this plan.

## **2.2 Post-Construction Monitoring Objectives**

Post-construction monitoring will be conducted to meet the following objectives:

- to document the species and number of individuals of bird and bat fatalities during the spring, summer, and late-fall during the first year of project operations;

- to estimate the level of take of birds and bats during the first two years of operation based on the results of standardized searches, searcher efficiency trials, scavenger carcass removal trails; and a search area correction factor (if necessary); and

- to determine if fatality events are uniform across the project area.

## **2.3 Standardized Mortality Searches**

All 23 turbines will be searched for the mortality monitoring during the first two years of project operations.  Individual turbines will be searched every three days during the spring (April 15 to June 1) and fall (August 1 to October 15) migration periods, based on recent fatality survey requests by MDIFW.

Parallel transects will be established at 4-meter (13 feet) intervals that span the entirety of each turbine search area.  Turbine searches will be completed during three survey days per week, typically consisting of seven to eight turbines per day. Searches will generally be scheduled for the same three days each week (Monday through Friday).

For each turbine, standardized search areas will be established and will include all leveled, graded laydown areas,  adjacent stable side slopes, and adjacent road sections.  Several post-construction avian and bat mortality studies have indicated that focusing search efforts on the cleared area surrounding each turbine is sufficient (Arnett et al., 2005; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; Erickson et al., 2003).  The majority of fatalities have been shown to occur within the tip height distance measured along the ground from the base of the turbines (Poulton and Erickson, 2010).  According to Poulton and Erickson (2010), bat carcasses have generally occurred within a distance equal to 50% of the tip height.  Further monitoring studies at wind project sites demonstrate that carcasses primarily occur within the area that is roughly equivalent to the height of the turbine hub, and the majority of bat fatalities are located within an even smaller area around the turbine (Young et al., 2005).

Personnel trained and experienced in proper search techniques will conduct the standardized mortality searches.  Searchers will walk along each transect at a rate of approximately 45 to 60 meters per minute, visually scanning approximately 2 meters on each side for casualties.  Search area and speed may be adjusted by habitat and terrain type after evaluation of the first searcher efficiency trial; however, a rate of 45 to 60 meters per minute is a standard search speed.  All turbines designated to be searched on a given day will be searched within 8 hours after sunrise, weather permitting.

During searches, all carcasses discovered (intact or scavenged) will be documented on standardized field forms.  When a dead bat or bird is found, the searcher will place a flag near the carcass and continue the search.  After searching the entire plot, the searcher will return to each carcass to record the information described below (Section 2.3.1).

Carcasses will be collected under the appropriate state and federal permits and will be individually bagged, labeled, and frozen.  Carcasses will be retained in a freezer at the Operations and Maintenance facility and may be used in searcher efficiency and scavenger carcass removal trials.  In the event that a federally or state-listed species carcass is discovered, the appropriate agency will be contacted, and the carcass will be submitted to the agency.  If a large-scale fatality event (i.e., more than five carcasses at one turbine or more than 20 carcasses found across the entire project area in one survey day) is observed, the MDIFW will be notified within 24 hours.  If an injured bird or bat is discovered, the animal will be transported to a local, certified wildlife rehabilitator, when possible.  Surveyors and operations personnel will be supplied with a handling protocol for injured birds and bats.

Any bat exhibiting signs of white-nose syndrome will be reported to the MDIFW and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) within 48 hours.  Carcasses of threatened or endangered bat species (e.g., Indiana bat, small-footed _Myotis_ , etc.) will not be used for searcher efficiency trials.  All carcasses of _Myotis_ sp _._ will be photographed with a digital camera, and those that cannot be positively identified in the field will be retained and frozen for later identification to eliminate the possibility of misidentifying a threatened or endangered species.  Collection and delivery of state or federal endangered, threatened, or protected species will be coordinated with the USFWS and state agencies.

Maintenance personnel will be informed of the timing of standardized searches and will be trained on the mortality reporting protocol in the event that a carcass or injured animal is discovered.  Carcasses found outside of the standardized searches will be documented and collected but will be reported separately from carcasses found during standard searches.  Incidental carcasses will not be used for estimates of take. Operations personnel will be instructed on the handling and notification requirements for these occurrences.

## **2.3.1 Recording Data**

Searchers will record data on standardized datasheets.  Each survey day, the following information will be recorded: personnel present; descriptions of weather conditions the preceding night (further details provided below); current weather conditions; turbines searched; overall timeframe of searches for the date; incidental wildlife observations; and general comments.  In regards to incidental wildlife observations, data recorded will consist of date, time and location of the observation,

observer name, species, and type of observation (e.g., live animal, track, scat, vocalization).

Nightly weather conditions will also be monitored and recorded throughout the survey period via the National Weather Service website (www.weather.gov).  Wind speed and direction, barometric pressure, and temperature will be recorded at an on-site met tower and/or by an anemometer on a turbine nacelle.  Additional weather parameters will be recorded by the field biologist from a location in proximity to the project on nights prior to fatality searches.  These parameters will include cloud type, percent cloud cover, general ceiling height (obtained from local Weather Service forecasts or from local airports), relative visibility, moon phase, precipitation, and any notable weather events (passing of storms or fronts).

Data pertaining to each turbine searched during a survey event will also be recorded, regardless of whether or not casualties are discovered.  Information will include: vegetation and general ground cover conditions (including vegetation type, percent coverage within search areas, vegetation height, and wet or dry substrate); timeframe of search effort; personnel present; and general results of the search.

For each casualty located, standard data will be documented.  Prior to handling, carcasses will be photographed as found, and the location documented using a GPS unit.  Additional information recorded will consist of the following: a standardized individual identification number for the carcass; date, time, and location of discovery (including corresponding turbine number); perpendicular distance from the transect line to the carcass; azimuth from turbine; distance to turbine using a laser range finder; vegetation class in which the carcass was found;

species/age/gender/ reproductive condition (when possible); carcass position (faceup or down, sprawled out or balled up); estimated time of death (e.g. <1 day, < 2 days); observer name; and comments on observations.

The condition of the carcass will be recorded according to the following categories:

- **Intact** : a completely intact carcass that is not badly decomposed and shows no sign of being consumed by a predator or scavenger.

- **Scavenged** : an entire carcass displaying signs of being partially consumed by a predator or scavenger or a portion of a carcass in one location (e.g., wings, skeletal remains, legs, pieces of skin, etc.).

- **Feather spot** : 10 or more feathers or two primary feathers at one location indicating predation or scavenging.

## **2.4 Visibility Class Mapping**

Vegetation conditions within search areas will be monitored on a weekly basis throughout the growing season.  Monitoring plots will be pre-established at locations that represent the range of vegetation and common growing conditions in the project area.  The height and density of vegetation in these plots will be monitored to determine when the period of accelerated early season growth is complete.  When this period ends, the vegetation at each turbine search area will be mapped by visibility class using a GPS unit.

Visibility class designations will adhere to the methodology described in Martin et al. (2012) and presented in Table 1.  Visibility classes are assigned based on vegetative cover and will subsequently be used as a variable in the overall mortality rate estimator (e.g., Huso et al., 2012; Huso, 2010).  In addition to visibility class mapping, percent of ground cover, height of ground cover, habitat type, and slope will be measured at each study plot to determine visibility classes and their combined influence on carcass detectability (Arnett et al., 2009).

## **2.5 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Searcher efficiency will be quantified to adjust the estimate of total bat and bird fatalities for detection bias using methods similar to Poulton and Erickson (2010). Searcher efficiency rates will be estimated by randomly placing bird and bat carcasses within the defined study area across the four survey seasons.  These trials will be temporally distributed throughout the study period.

A target number of 50 total carcasses will be placed during trials over the course of the survey year. Carcasses used for efficiency trials will be obtained during earlier search efforts.  However, if too few carcasses are available, then surrogate species of a similar size and appearance as native species will be obtained.  Carcasses will be placed in the various ground cover types occurring within search areas.  The percent

of carcasses found during trials will be used to estimate the level of bird and bat take during the study period.

A random numbers table will be used to generate a list of random turbine sites, azimuths, and distances from the turbine to determine placement of the test carcasses.  Bird and bat carcasses will consist of different sizes and will be in various stages of decay to account for this source of variation in searcher detectability. Carcasses will be placed the night before or on the morning of searches (prior to arrival of survey personnel) at sites scheduled to be searched that day.  Survey personnel will be unaware of the timing of efficiency trials.

Personnel placing carcasses will note the placement of each trial carcass, thereby allowing carcasses to be identified as study specimens once found by the searcher or be retrieved at the end of the day if not detected by the searcher.  The percent of test carcasses discovered by the searcher will be documented on standardized datasheets.  In the event that a trial carcass is determined to be removed by a scavenger prior to the standard carcass search, that carcass will be removed from the trials and not counted in the final results.

## **2.6 Carcass Removal Trials**

Carcass removal trials are generally required to correct for biases introduced by the decay or scavenging of carcasses between survey events.  Carcass removal rate trials will be conducted during each survey season and will be completed independently of the searcher efficiency trials.  A target total of 50 carcasses will be placed within all available ground cover types within search areas.  Fresh bird and bat carcasses of native species will be discreetly marked and monitored until they are removed by scavengers or completely decomposed.  Carcasses will be checked during the first seven days after they are placed, then again on days 10, 14, 24, 28, and on additional days if necessary.

During the trial periods, the status of carcasses, including all evidence of scavenging or decomposition, will be documented on standardized field forms.  The carcass removal data will be used to estimate the percent of carcasses that remain detectable in search areas during the interval between standardized searches.

## **2.7 Analysis and Reporting**

Post-construction mortality monitoring data will be summarized by season and will consist of species, date, turbine number, carcass condition, and weather conditions for each bird and bat fatality.  The relationship between fatalities (including

carcasses found during searches and incidentally) and the season in which the fatalities occurred will be examined for trends.  Correlations between mortality events and nighttime weather conditions when fatality events were suspected to have occurred (i.e., fresh carcasses discovered during searches and incidentally that can be attributed to the previous night) will also be examined.

Additional statistical analyses will be conducted to assess trends in the spatial distribution of carcasses at individual turbines and between turbines.  The location of carcasses found at individual turbines (including fatalities discovered during searches and incidentally) will be analyzed to identify any potential trends in the spatial distribution of carcasses around the turbines.  Components of within-turbine spatial distribution that will be examined consist of distance and bearing of carcasses from the turbine, evenness of distribution of fatalities at individual turbines, and the vegetation visibility class in which carcasses were found. Components of between-turbine spatial distribution that will be examined consist of total number of fatalities at each turbine searched, number of fatalities by topographical setting (crest, mid-slope, or saddle), number of fatalities at mid-string verses end-string turbines; and number of fatalities at Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lit and FAA unlit turbines.

The number of carcasses found during the standard searches, corrected by search area and the percent of carcasses found by the observer as determined by the searcher efficiency trials, will be used to estimate bird and bat take during the study period.  Results will be presented as the number of bird and bat fatalities per turbine and per megawatt per study period.  To estimate mortality, it is likely that the Huso Estimator (Huso et al., 2012; Huso, 2010) will be used, provided that the total data points collected meet the requirements necessary for using this formula.  Alternative fatality estimators are available if the data is deemed insufficient for the Huso Estimator.

## **2.7.1 Search Area Correction**

In some locations, the turbine search area may be significantly reduced by topography, and carcasses may land in unsearchable forested areas adjacent to the cleared turbine pad search areas.  In such circumstances, a correction factor can be applied to the number of carcasses found at these turbines.  The correction factor would estimate the number of carcasses that may have fallen in non-searchable areas at abbreviated search plots, based on the number of carcasses observed within the searchable area.  A density-weighted correction factor based on methods described in other studies (Jain et al., 2009; Fiedler et al., 2007) would provide a per-

turbine adjustment for the total number of bird and bat carcasses that would have been found within the standard search radius for each turbine if the entire area was searchable.

## **Curtailment Plan**

## **Curtailment Plan Weaver Wind Project**

Prepared for: First Wind, LLC 129 Middle Street 3rd Floor Portland, Maine 04101

Prepared by: Stantec Consulting Services Inc. 30 Park Drive Topsham, Maine 04086

## **CURTAILMENT PLAN**

The most recent research at operating wind farms within the eastern United States indicates that curtailment of wind turbines at low wind speeds has the potential to reduce bat fatality. Curtailment consists of altering (delaying) the operation of a wind turbine so that it begins generating energy at a specified wind speed greater than the manufacturer’s “cut-in” wind speed (e.g., manufacturer’s cut-in speed of 3.0 or 3.5 meters per second [m/s], depending on the turbine model).  When turbines are programmed to curtail and wind speeds are between the manufacturer’s cut-in speed and some specified, higher curtailment cut-in speed (e.g., 5.0 m/s), turbine blades can be pitched parallel to the wind such that the rotation of the rotor (the 3 blades and the nose cone) is limited to < 2-3 rotations per minute (rpm) (and typically < 1 rpm). Such low rotor rpm results in blade tip speeds that do not pose a collision danger to bats.

Studies assessing the effectiveness of curtailment have generally focused on late summer/early fall, the time period when bat fatalities throughout North America have been observed to be most common (Arnett et al. 2013).  These studies have incorporated various combinations of low wind speed, temperature, and time of night to account for the times and weather conditions when bat activity, and presumably collision risk, is greatest (Hayes 1997, Arnett et al. 2006, Arnett et al. 2010, Arnett et al. 2013, Reynolds 2006, Kunz 2004, Kunz and Lumsden 2003 as cited by Young et al. 2011).

First Wind, LLC proposes to curtail operation of the Weaver Wind Project (Project) to reduce potential bat fatalities, as described below.  This curtailment plan is based on the most current information available from post-construction fatality monitoring and curtailment assessment studies in Maine, and across North America.

The proposed curtailment plan varies from the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (MDIFW) recommendations in _Maine Turbine Curtailment Requirements to Decrease Bat Mortality Policy (January 2014)_ , as described in their _Curtailment Policy and Wind Power Preconstruction Study Recommendations, updated April, 2014._ The MDIFW recommendations call for turbines to be curtailed when all of the following criteria are met:  (1) from April 20 to October 15; (2) from 0.5 hour before sunset to 0.5 hour after sunrise; and (3) when average wind speed (10-minute interval) at the hub height of a turbine is 6 m/s or below.  These curtailment parameters exceed what has been determined to reliably reduce bat fatalities in numerous studies, and would result in an unnecessary cost to the Project (and loss of renewable energy generation) without providing any demonstrated reduction in bat fatalities.  First Wind’s proposed plan is more focused, and will accomplish equal protection for bats with less unnecessary waste of renewable generation.

## _Time of Year_

An abundance of fatality data from sites across the eastern United States demonstrate that a very small percentage of bat fatality occurs in April, May, June, and October.  For example, a total of 19 bat fatalities were found during 2013 monitoring at the Bull Hill Wind Project.  Of these, none were found in April; 2 tree-roosting bats were found in late-May, no bats were found in June, and no bat fatalities were found after September 21, 2013 (Stantec 2014).  During 2014 monitoring at the Bull Hill Wind Project, 3 tree-roosting bats were found between August 18 and September 18 (Stantec unpubl.); no bats were found outside of this window.  Furthermore, 86% of bat fatalities documented at operational wind projects in Maine from 2007 to 2013, during 7,690 turbine searches, were found between July 1 and September 30 (Table 1, Stantec unpubl.).  Ultimately, the results cited above from the 12 seasons of observations at 8 projects in Maine consistently indicate that bats are at risk of collision primarily from July 1 to September 30, with minimal risk of collision outside of this period.  First Wind therefore proposes to curtail turbines on nights between July 1 and September 30, which is the demonstrated peak period of bat fatality at projects in Maine and across the Northeast.

## _Time of Night_

Bat acoustic data from the region generally indicate that far less than 1 percent of bat activity occurs after sunrise.  Similarly, a very small proportion of bat acoustic calls are recorded in the half hour before sunset.  For example, during acoustic monitoring at the Weaver Wind Project from mid-April to mid-October in 2014, there were no bat calls recorded prior to sunset while detectors operated from 18:00 to 8:00 (detectors were recording at least an hour before sunset for the duration of the monitoring period, with the exception of the last week of surveys in midOctober).  Figure 1 shows the number of bat sequences recorded per hour for the duration of the acoustic survey at Weaver.  Accordingly, First Wind proposes to curtail from sunset to sunrise.

Figure 1.  Number of bat calls recorded per hour at the Weaver Wind Project, mid-April to midOctober, 2014.

## _Temperature_

Bat activity has been demonstrated to be correlated not only with wind speed but also with ambient temperature (and perhaps several other atmospheric conditions) that can be incorporated into a refined curtailment strategy that is data driven.  Based on a curtailment period of July 1 to September 30, inclusion of a temperature threshold (i.e., above 50 degrees Fahrenheit) is not recommended because nightly temperatures in Maine rarely dip below 50 degrees during this period.  However, should the curtailment window include spring and fall time periods when bat activity is naturally limited, then it may be appropriate to reconsider including a temperature threshold such that curtailment occurs only on warm nights within those seasons when bats would be active.

## _Curtailment cut-in speed_

Bat Conservation International (BCI) recently published a summary of 10 studies in North America that tested the effectiveness of different curtailment strategies at reducing bat fatalities at wind facilities in North America (Arnett et al. 2013).  There were 8 studies in the United States and 2 studies in Canada summarized, at the following locations:

- Alberta, Canada

- Casselman, Pennsylvania

- Mount Storm, West Virginia

- Fowler Ridge, Indiana

- Sheffield, Vermont

- Wolfe Island, Ontario

- Beech Ridge, West Virginia

- Criterion, Maryland

- Anonymous Project 1, USFWS Region 3

- Anonymous Project 2, USFWS Region 8

These curtailment studies were conducted between July and mid-October.  Most studies found at least a 50% reduction in bat fatalities when turbine cut-in speed was increased by at least 1.5 m/s above the normal manufacturer’s cut-in speed.  Five studies looked at bat fatalities at turbines with cut-in speeds of 5.0 m/s and higher; however none evaluated the incremental (e.g., increasing by 1 m/s) benefit of raising the cut-in speed.  Where decreases in bat fatalities have been observed above 5.0 m/s, these reductions are markedly less than the reductions achieved at 5.0 m/s.  In most cases, the greatest percent reduction in bat fatalities was

achieved by raising the cut-in speed from “normal” (3.0, 3.5, or 4.0 m/s) to 4.5 or 5.0 m/s.  Studies that implemented feathered blades, or a low-speed idling of blades at or below cut-in speed with no other curtailment treatment, also demonstrated significant reductions in bat fatality (Baerwald and Barclay 2009, Young et al. 2011).

The Sheffield, Vermont; Pinnacle, West Virginia; and Wolf Ridge, Oklahoma and Texas wind projects are curtailment studies that have more recently become available. The Sheffield Wind Project investigated the effects of a 6.0 m/s cut-in speed compared to the manufacturer’s cut-in speed at 4 m/s.  The 2012 study at Sheffield indicated the increased cut-in speed reduced bat fatalities by 60% (Martin et al. 2013).  However, in 2013, there was no statistical difference between 4 m/s and 6 m/s in the reduction of bat fatalities (Martin et al. 2014).  At the Pinnacle Wind Project in 2012, a 72.2 % reduction in bat fatalities was observed (when the proportion of the night when wind speed was between 3 and 5 m/s was 50%) with 5 m/s treatments (for all night treatments, but not for half-night treatments which were also tested) compared to fully operational turbines (Hein et al. 2013).  This reduction was 81.7% when an outlier night was removed from the model (Hein et al. 2013). At the Wolf Ridge Wind Project in Texas and Oklahoma, there was no significant difference in the reduction of fatalities between a flat 5.0 regime and a variable regime based on wind direction that included cut-in speeds as high as 6.5 m/s (Hale 2014).  In summary, while bat fatality reductions were observed at 1 project during the first study year using a 6.0 m/s cut-in speed, these other 2 studies showed substantial reductions in bat fatality using a 5.0 m/s cut-in speed.

Based on the most current curtailment assessment information, as well as the seasonal timing of fatalities observed during 2 years of monitoring at the Bull Hill Wind Project, First Wind believes that a 5.0 m/s curtailment regime from July 1 to September 30 will be effective at reducing the risk of bat fatalities at the Project, and will reduce unnecessary costs associated with curtailment on operations.

First Wind agrees that curtailment, when properly applied, has the potential to meaningfully reduce bat fatalities. The concept of curtailment using site- and regional-specific information (also referred to as Smart Curtailment) is an evolving science that is being investigated in several

ongoing studies.  First Wind suggests that the initial curtailment protocol (including seasonal time period as well as nightly time periods) be as proposed above, with an allowance for adjustments to be made in the future based on actual observed fatalities, in cooperation with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (MDEP).  For example, if fatalities of listed species or species proposed for listing are documented outside of the July 1 to September 30 time period during post-construction monitoring, First Wind will, in consultation with MDEP, expand the curtailment timeframe for future years to include the period when the fatalities occurred.  In this manner the curtailment regime can be tailored to best fit the documented risk of bat fatalities at the site.  This approach provides greater potential for protecting bats while minimizing lost generation.

In the future, First Wind recommends emerging data be incorporated into project-specific adaptive management at the Project, as it becomes available.  For example, recent studies using infrared videography show greatest levels of bat activity in proximity to turbines when the blades are not spinning or when they are spinning very slowly (Hein 2014). Researchers have hypothesized that fatalities occur when wind speeds increase slightly and turbines begin spinning unexpectedly, catching bats by surprise.  If true, operational adjustments such as slowing the ramp-up speed and/or extending the decision to resume normal operations may be more important in reducing bat fatalities than increasing cut-in speed (Hein 2014).  Further, if emerging technologies such as high-frequency audio or infra-red visual deterrents are proven to effectively reduce bat fatalities at rates that match or exceed curtailment, then projects may have the option to implement these methods in exchange for removing curtailment requirements.
